speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: asked the Minister for Manpower given the recent issues highlighted at the Westlite Jalan Tukang Dormitory, how will the Ministry be holding the dormitory operators and their corporate clients even more accountable for delivering an acceptable level of care to our foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) what is the overall vaccination rate for all dormitory residents; (b) what is the vaccination rate at the Westlite Jalan Tukang Dormitory; and (c) what proportion of Chinese workers living at the Westlite Jalan Tukang Dormitory have been vaccinated before they arrived in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) with regard to the Westlite Jalan Tukang Domitory, whether there is non-segregation of workers who tested positive for COVID-19, substandard quality of food provided and lack of access to medical support; and (b) if so, who will be held responsible for these lapses in the migrant workers’ living conditions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) whether the Government will review its current stay-in requirements for workers in dormitories who are infected with COVID-19, bearing in mind that such accommodation typically requires a number of workers to live in close proximity when sharing dormitory rooms and common facilities like toilets, bathrooms and wash basins; and (b) whether such accommodation may allow for easier virus transmission as well as promoting anxiety and fear of infection among those sharing the same rooms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) what is being done to monitor and evaluate the quality of food catered for migrant workers, including nutritional value and cultural appropriateness, food hygiene and safety standards; (b) on average, what is the time gap between production and consumption of such food; and (c) what enforcement actions have been taken against employers who fail to comply with the requisite food standards.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In line with the shift to the Home Recovery Programme in our community, the dormitories have phased in a Dormitory Recovery Programme since 2 October in the transition towards "living with COVID-19".

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ninety-eight percent of dormitory residents are fully vaccinated and most are below the age of 60.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A vast majority of recent infections are asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Forty-five larger dormitories now have dedicated blocks or rooms set aside within their compounds as Dormitory Recovery Facilities (DRFs).

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: COVID-19-positive vaccinated workers who are asymptomatic or only mildly symptomatic can recuperate and be monitored in DRFs while being segregated from other workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Additionally, we have set up three Centralised Recovery Facilities (CRFs) in the larger dormitories to cater for workers who do not have access to the 45 DRFs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will expand these recovery capacities if needed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have also aligned testing protocols in the DRFs and CRFs with the rest of our community.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Workers who test negative on their supervised Antigen Rapid Tests (ARTs) after 72 hours of isolation can be discharged.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Workers are given thermometers and oximeters to monitor themselves three times a day and report these numbers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A recovery buddy is designated in each room to help with the dissemination of information and to monitor the health of fellow migrant workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The majority were discharged by Day 7 and about half of them were discharged by Day 4.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The small minority who developed symptoms continued to have access to medical support through daily sick parades at our regional medical centres or telemedicine consultations which are available 24/7.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mobile Clinical Teams may also be deployed to DRFs or CRFs with high report sick rate to augment access to primary care.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The workers appreciate the convenience of dormitory recovery since they can return quickly to their rooms on discharge and resume work very rapidly.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: About half of them are employed by Sembcorp Marine and almost all of them are newly arrived workers from China in the last three to four months.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These workers were offered vaccination under our national vaccination programme, with a small number taking it up.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The employer has since clarified that these workers had been vaccinated in their home country before arriving in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The vaccination status of these workers needed to be verified through a serology test and WHO-EUL vaccination documentation before we can register them as being vaccinated in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOM has been working with the employer to expedite the verification.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To date, about 60% of the Sembcorp Marine workers have been verified to have received WHO-EUL-approved vaccines, while a number have not been vaccinated with WHO-EUL vaccines and we encourage them to be vaccinated in Singapore for their own protection.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Following the implementation of the Dormitory Recovery Programme on 2 October, the dormitory operator began adjusting to these new protocols.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On 10 October, there were 174 newly detected Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) and Antigen Rapid Test (ART) positive cases.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, the dormitory operator had difficulty processing the sudden surge of workers that needed to be conveyed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The next day, on 11 October, some key members of the dormitory staff did not come to work as they themselves had tested positive.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Assurance, Care and Engagement Group or ACE officers on the ground stepped in on that day to assist the operator.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This happened while the team was trying to process the previous surge, and the dormitory operator struggled to process the high volume.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While ACE officers tried to assist the operator between 11 and 12 October, it, too, did not put in enough resources during this time to triage, process and convey the COVID-19-positive workers before the second surge on 13 October.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, we doubled the number of officers to manage the conveyance of all infected workers from the dormitory such that, by the evening of 13 October, about 70% of the workers needing conveyance had been sent to the appropriate recovery or isolation facilities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: By the next day, on 14 October, the backlog was cleared.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In addition, ACE officers, together with the employer and dormitory operator, engaged the workers and assured them that their feedback would be looked into and there would be timely conveyance of infected individuals.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The workers calmed down and returned to their rooms.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: ACE also deployed a mobile clinical team to the dormitory to augment the existing medical services that were already available to the residents at Westlite Jalan Tukang Dormitory through the regional medical centres and telemedicine.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: All those who wanted to seek medical attention were seen by the medical team on site on the same day.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This helped to reduce the waiting time and allay much of the fears and anxieties that the workers experienced.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The situation has been calm in the dormitory since 13 October.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Over the following days and weeks, ACE officers, together with the employer and dormitory operator, continued to be at the dormitory every day to engage the workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In fact, over the last two weeks, ACE has introduced more videos and infographics to better explain Singapore’s strategy for dealing with COVID-19 and the recovery process in our dormitories, in view that the newly-arrived workers at the dormitory were used to a different COVID-19 management strategy in their home country.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In particular, there are now videos of migrant workers sharing their recovery journey and assuring their fellow migrant workers, as well as videos of doctors answering common questions from migrant workers in their own native languages.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I urge employers and dormitory operators to do more to help our workers adjust to the new normal, communicate changes that will affect workers’ well-being and actively address potential knowledge gaps of their workers and residents.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We also call on workers who are not vaccinated or not verified – if they are vaccinated overseas – to complete their vaccination or verification as soon as possible as this will protect them from serious illnesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOM and sector agencies will monitor this progress.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We also saw many of our partners coming in to support the workers after the incident on 13 October.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We are very grateful and encouraged by the outpouring of support by the Chinese business community, the Chinese Embassy, NGOs like HealthServe, Migrant Workers' Centre and the wider community.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is testimony to the civic-mindedness and big-heartedness of our community here in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is similar to how, at the height of the pandemic last year, MOM worked with the High Commissions of India and of Bangladesh, as well as various NGOs to support our migrant workers, including celebrating festive occasions with them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We thank all parties for their contributions and donations, and we will continue to work together to care for our migrant workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The employer has reported that they have made improvements to the food and the feedback from the workers has been positive.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the employer's part, workers were upset and had raised issues about food quality and hygiene.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the dormitory operator's part, they struggled to cope with the surge in numbers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On ACE's part, we stepped in but did not put in sufficient resources in time to resolve the problem.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Following the incident, all parties have diligently addressed the issues, restored calm to the dormitory and to the workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have also conducted a thorough review and tightened up the processes, especially for escalating and calling in more resources to deal with a surge in cases that need to be conveyed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: ACE has also tightened up coordination and communication with dormitory operators and employers when handling mass testing exercises and a surge in cases.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Investigations into failures to fulfil regulatory obligations, for example, in food safety and hygiene issues, are ongoing.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: All parties across our more than 1,300 dormitories, whether it is dormitory operators, employers and ACE officers on the ground, play important roles to support the recovery of our migrant workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will learn from this episode and continue to strengthen the partnership with all stakeholders and community partners to ensure the well-being of our migrant workers as we transit into endemicity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have a question pertaining to MOM's ACE Group, which was a new division set up last year, taking over from the inter-agency task force, and it pertains to the deployment of forward assurance and support teams.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear from the Senior Minister of State's chronology that, between 10 and 12 October, there were gaps.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I seek confirmation from the Senior Minister of State as to the manpower situation within ACE itself, whether there are enough individuals and teams to cover not just this particular dormitory but the vast number of dormitories in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second question pertains to the first part of what the Senior Minister of State shared with regard to the Dormitory Recovery Programme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand from individuals in HealthServe that mental health concerns are becoming more noteworthy.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The first one is on whether we have enough ACE officers to cover the number of dormitories we have.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There will never be enough to go around on a regular basis, to plant people in all 1,300 dormitories.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: How we go about doing this is to leverage the partnership we have with our stakeholders: the dormitory operators, the employers and, of course, we have volunteers within the migrant worker community, the friends of ACE, where they are also ambassadors, where they are migrant workers themselves who have been here for some time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They are trained and equipped with some of the basic knowledge to share information with their fellow workers, to help spread the message and also to help to collate feedback and channel this upwards to all of us.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, in a way, it is about leveraging the multiplier effect of everyone pitching their hands in and working together.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As the Member will appreciate, to have operations within 1,300 dormitories, big and small, with different phases perhaps of infection, of liberalisation of going to the community or going to work.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The work necessary to coordinate across all the different stakeholders as well as to ensure that when a case is detected; documentation of the COVID-19-positive result; churning out a nominal roll, a name list; communicating the need for conveyance and then for the team to arrange for the necessary transportation; having also the receiving party at the other end, at the dormitory recovery facilities (DRFs) or the centralised recovery facilities (CRFs), for example, is a necessary complex process that involves quite a bit of communication and coordination.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, we do make sure that our ACE officers are prioritised in terms of going to the dormitories that need help rather than have them spread thin over all the many places.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In a way, it is about risk-strategising and prioritisation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: At this moment, we are working with what we have.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: When there is a need to, if there is a real major surge in demand that we need to augment our numbers, we will look at increasing the number of ACE officers that we need to deploy.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The second question pertains to how much more we can do in liberalising community visits for our dormitory workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I must say that our dormitory workers have been very, very patient and they have actually gone through a lot in the last one and a half years or so.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In the past month or so, we have started a community pilot: visits for workers to go into the community.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We started with about 500 and then, with the success of that pilot, you will see in today's newspaper that an announcement has been made over the weekend.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, there are less restrictions going to recreation centres.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That, again, offers another outlet for them to access services, to also have the necessary interactions that they need at the recreation centres, on top of the community visits that we are liberalising.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The first one is, MWC has been working with MOM to help the management of dormitories.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For this particular incident, why were the other agencies or NGOs not brought on board to support ACE for that few days?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Is it linked to certain critical priorities that MOM might have?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The other supplementary question is on the vaccination of these workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we prevent and enhance the arrival of such unvaccinated workers for future batches?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the first question relating to why the NGOs were not brought in earlier, let me explain that when the surge in cases occurred, the topmost priority in the minds of our ACE officers who went in on 9 and 10 October was to augment the dorm operators, the topmost priority was really to do the processing and to do the triaging of those who may have need for medical care.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On 9 October, a mobile clinical team was deployed onsite to help cope with the load of increased number of residents who might need medical attention or seek consultation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is about making sure that our team on the ground focused on what is the most urgent need and that was to take care of the medical conditions – make sure they are well, make sure they are safe medically, first.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The next priority then was to ensure that we can stitch the logistics together and make sure there is enough conveyancing capacity to bring these workers to the necessary isolation facilities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That situation with COVID-19 cases going up in the dorm, it would not be appropriate to allow NGOs to be exposed to the risk of infection in a dorm like this.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Because the work then was about medical care, was about conveyancing.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is not necessarily something that the NGOs have the capability to provide as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, that is the reason why in the first few days, our ACE officers were working with resources we have with the dorm operators to make sure that these important needs are met.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In fact, the Embassy came in only on 14 October, for example, to also provide some of these supplies like masks, hand sanitisers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These were useful as a psychological boost for our workers; but by themselves, they would not be able to address the medical needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is quite clear from the sequence of events, the team was on the ground early on to try and manage the medical situation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As to the second question of why there were so many so-called unvaccinated workers coming to Singapore, you must remember that this happened when the workers came in three, four months ago.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The earlier batches came in at about mid-July and then, another bulk of them came in at around August.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: At that time, we were still in the "zero COVID-19" situation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We were trying to contain the numbers., but we had imposed Not to Land (NTL) on some of the high-risk countries.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For low-risk countries, we did not impose NTL for them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: China is one of those countries where they have very low COVID-19 numbers and we did not impose NTL on China workers coming in at that time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: At that time also, our dorms were not into the endemic posture, and so, even if the workers turned out not to be vaccinated, there was a way to keep them safe.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But in this process, by October, we were transiting to more of an endemic posture.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Those workers, who came in earlier on when we were still pursuing a zero-COVID-19 type of strategy, were therefore caught in that transition if their vaccination status was not up to the mark in terms of personal protection.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That is why we are encouraging both the workers and employers to get this thing sorted out as soon as possible and for those who are yet to be vaccinated, to get them vaccinated.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This would be an adjustment that we are making from today onwards, in line with our endemic posture to make sure that anybody who is applying for a work pass, we make sure that they are vaccinated before allowing them to come in.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, this is a gap that will gradually narrow over time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We are now digesting the group of people who came in just before that, who may then have a certain vaccination gap that we need to fill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have two supplementary questions just on food quality.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I know SFA is investigating the food quality claims around this particular incident.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I am not sure whether such a claim is absolutely correct that this complaint has been going on for years and years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These workers have been here for less than four months.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Regulations that apply to dorm caterers, yes, I think it is a standard that we apply across to all catering, whether it is to the dorms or for other public consumption.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Regarding feedback for standards of food hygiene, there are various avenues in which the workers can feed back.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Through this app, they can feedback directly to MOM, to ACE, for example, on any issues relating to their dorm conditions, including food.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, that is something through which workers have direct access to our agencies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The second thing is that there are volunteer groups, NGOs who are in regular contact with our workers – what we call Friends of ACE – when they are organising activities, when they interact with the workers, this is again another channel of feedback.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I must say our NGOs are very, very much pro-workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They will not hesitate to tell us when there is any feedback that they receive regarding sub-standard accommodation or food.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These are foreign workers themselves, staying in the dormitories, who have been here in Singapore for many years; some of them, even for a decade.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They are quite familiar with the setting, they are quite familiar with the standards that are to be expected on a day-to-day basis and they again, form another channel of feedback to the relevant authorities and to the NGOs as well, if standards were to drop.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The final one is that MWC runs a hotline where all foreign workers who face challenges and they cannot get through to the employers or to anyone else, can call this hotline where they can directly give feedback to MWC as well as the ambassadors who speak their native languages to collate all the feedback.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I think there is no shortage of feedback.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Clearly, some of these things, if there were language barriers, we need to look into that.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In this case, I think they were very much newly arrived workers, they may not be exactly familiar with many of these resources opened to them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If there are investigations that show that employers have actually violated any of these obligations, we will take them to task.
